# Chapter 7: Sharing and Collaborating on Files in Teams

## The End of the "Final_v2_Updated_FINAL.docx" Nightmare

Imagine you are working on a project proposal with three colleagues. In the old way of working, you would write a draft in Word, save it, and email it to your team. Your colleague, Sarah, would make changes, save it as "Proposal_Sarah_Edits," and email it back. Then Mark would add his notes and save it as "Proposal_FINAL_v2." 

Within two days, you have five different versions of the same document scattered across four different email threads. You spend more time trying to figure out which file is the "current" one than actually writing the proposal.

Microsoft Teams eliminates this chaos. Instead of sending copies of a file back and forth, you store one single version of a file in a shared space. Everyone works on that same file at the same time. This is called **Co-authoring**, and it is the engine that drives collaboration in the modern digital workspace.

## Uploading Files to Teams and Channels

To collaborate, you first need to get your documents into the Teams environment. You can do this in two primary ways: uploading to a specific conversation (a chat or channel post) or uploading directly to the file storage area.

### Uploading via a Conversation
When you are chatting in a channel or a private chat, you might want to share a document that is relevant to the current discussion.

1. Navigate to the **Channel** or **Chat** where you want to share the file.
2. In the message compose box at the bottom, look for the **Paperclip icon (Attach)**.
3. Select **Upload from my computer** (or choose from your OneDrive if your files are already in the cloud).
4. Select the file from your folders and click **Open**.
5. Type a message to give your team context (e.g., "Here is the budget draft for review") and press **Enter** to send.

By doing this, the file is automatically uploaded to the team's storage, and a link to that file is placed directly in the conversation for everyone to see.

### Uploading via the Files Tab
If you have a large batch of documents or want to organize files without sending a message, use the **Files tab**. Every channel in Teams has a dedicated Files tab located at the top of the window.

1. Select the **Team** and then the specific **Channel** where the files belong.
2. Click the **Files** tab at the top of the screen.
3. Click the **Upload** button.
4. Choose **Files** (for individual documents) or **Folder** (to upload an entire folder structure from your computer).
5. Select your items and click **Upload**.

**Pro Tip:** You can also simply "drag and drop" a file from your computer folder directly into the Files tab window to upload it instantly.

## Opening and Editing Shared Files

Once a file is uploaded to Teams, you don't need to download it to your computer to work on it. Downloading a file creates a "local copy," which defeats the purpose of collaboration because your changes won't be seen by others until you upload it again.

### Editing Within Teams
By default, when you click a file in the Files tab or a link in a chat, Teams opens the document inside the Teams window. This is the fastest way to make quick edits.

*   **Real-time Presence:** If other team members are in the document at the same time, you will see their initials or profile pictures in the top right corner. 
*   **Live Cursors:** You will see a colored cursor moving across the page, showing exactly where your colleague is typing. This prevents you from overwriting each other's work.
*   **Auto-Save:** You do not need to click a "Save" button. Every keystroke is saved automatically to the cloud.

### Opening in the Desktop App
While editing inside Teams is convenient, you might need the full power of the Microsoft 365 apps (like the advanced formatting tools in Word or complex data formulas in Excel).

1. Open the file in Teams.
2. Click the **Editing** button (or the three dots `...`) in the top toolbar.
3. Select **Open in Desktop App**.

The file will launch in the full version of Word, Excel, or PowerPoint on your computer. Because the file is hosted in Teams, the Desktop App still uses **Auto-Save**. Any change you make in the app is reflected instantly for everyone else viewing the file in Teams.

## Managing Documents with the Files Tab

The Files tab is more than just a list of documents; it is a full-scale file management system. Think of it as a shared digital filing cabinet for your team.

### Organizing with Folders
To keep your workspace from becoming cluttered, you can create a folder hierarchy.
1. In the **Files** tab, click **New** $\rightarrow$ **Folder**.
2. Give the folder a clear, descriptive name (e.g., "2024 Project Expenses").
3. You can move existing files into these folders by clicking the three dots `...` next to a file and selecting **Move to**, then choosing the destination folder.

### Basic File Actions
When you hover over a file or click the three dots `...` next to it, you have several management options:
*   **Rename:** Change the file name without breaking the link for other users.
*   **Copy:** Create a duplicate of the file.
*   **Delete:** Remove the file from the channel (it will move to the SharePoint recycle bin).
*   **Pin to Top:** If there is a document the team uses daily (like a Project Tracker), select **Pin to Top**. This keeps the file visible at the top of the list regardless of how many new files are added.

## Controlling Access and Permissions

Not every file should be open for everyone to edit. Sometimes you want a team member to read a document but not change it, or you may want to restrict a sensitive file to only a few people.

### Understanding Permissions
In Teams, permissions are generally inherited from the Team itself. If a person is a member of the Team, they typically have permission to edit files in that Team's channels. However, you can refine this.

### Setting Specific Permissions
To change who can see or edit a specific file:
1. Go to the **Files** tab.
2. Click the three dots `...` next to the file and select **Manage Access**.
3. A sidebar will appear showing who has access. You can change a user's status from **Can edit** to **Can view**.
4. If you want to share the file with someone who isn't in the Team, you can use the **Share** button to send a specific link with defined permissions (e.g., "People in your organization with the link can view").

## Recovering Work with Version History

One of the biggest fears in a collaborative environment is that someone might accidentally delete a critical paragraph or mess up a complex spreadsheet formula. **Version History** is the safety net that solves this problem.

Instead of saving multiple versions of a file (v1, v2, v3), Teams keeps a hidden log of every time the document was saved.

### How to Restore a Previous Version
If you realize that a file was corrupted or a mistake was made yesterday, follow these steps:

1. In the **Files** tab, click the three dots `...` next to the file.
2. Select **Open in SharePoint**. (SharePoint is the underlying technology that stores Teams files; this opens the file's "back end" in your web browser).
3. Right-click the file in the SharePoint list and select **Version History**.
4. A list of all previous versions will appear, timestamped and labeled with the name of the person who made the changes.
5. Hover over the version you want to recover and select **Restore**.

Once restored, that older version becomes the current version of the file for everyone in the Team.

## Scenario: The Monthly Report Workflow

To see how these features work together, let's look at a realistic workflow for a Marketing Team creating a monthly report.

1. **Upload:** The Team Lead creates a folder in the "Reports" channel called "October 2023" and uploads a blank Word template.
2. **Collaborate:** The Lead @mentions the team in the channel, asking them to add their updates. Three team members open the file simultaneously. One writes the "Social Media" section, another handles "Web Traffic," and the third adds "Budget" notes—all seeing each other's cursors in real-time.
3. **Refine:** The Lead opens the document in the **Desktop App** to apply professional branding and final formatting.
4. **Protect:** Once the report is finished, the Lead uses **Manage Access** to change the file to "View Only" so that no one accidentally alters the final version.
5. **Recover:** A week later, the Lead realizes a section was deleted by mistake. They use **Version History** to go back to the version from Tuesday and restore the missing text.

## Key Takeaways

*   **Co-authoring** allows multiple people to edit the same file simultaneously, eliminating the need for multiple email attachments.
*   **Uploading** can be done via the paperclip icon in a chat for immediate context, or via the **Files tab** for general organization.
*   **Editing** can happen directly inside Teams for speed, or in the **Desktop App** for advanced features; both options save changes automatically.
*   **The Files Tab** acts as the team's central repository, allowing for folder organization and the ability to **Pin** important documents.
*   **Permissions** can be adjusted via **Manage Access** to switch users from "Can edit" to "Can view."
*   **Version History** (accessed via SharePoint) allows you to view and restore previous versions of a document, protecting against accidental data loss.

# Chapter 8: Starting and Joining Meetings in Teams

## The Shift from Email to Instant Meetings

Imagine you are working on a project and realize you and a colleague have a fundamental misunderstanding about a deadline. You could send an email, wait two hours for a reply, send a follow-up, and spend the rest of the afternoon in a "text loop" that solves nothing. Or, you could start a meeting in seconds, see each other's faces, resolve the issue in three minutes, and get back to work.

This is the core power of meetings in Microsoft Teams. Whether it is a formal board meeting with twenty people or a quick "huddle" with one teammate, Teams transforms the way you communicate by moving conversations from static text to real-time interaction.

## Scheduling Your First Meeting

There are two primary ways to schedule a meeting depending on whether you are planning ahead or reacting to a conversation.

### Using the Calendar Tab
The **Calendar tab** is your central hub for time management. It syncs directly with your Outlook calendar, meaning any appointment you make in one will appear in the other.

1. Click the **Calendar** icon on the left-hand navigation bar (the sidebar you learned about in Chapter 3).
2. Select **New meeting** in the top right corner.
3. **Add a title:** Give your meeting a clear name (e.g., "Weekly Project Sync").
4. **Add required attendees:** Type the names of the people you want to invite. Teams will suggest names from your organization as you type.
5. **Set the date and time:** Use the dropdown menus to pick when the meeting starts and ends.
6. **Add a description:** In the large text box, you can add an agenda or notes so attendees know what to prepare.
7. Click **Send**. 

Once you click send, Teams automatically sends an email invitation to all attendees and places the event on their calendars.

### Scheduling from a Chat
Sometimes, while using the **Persistent chat** features covered in Chapter 5, you realize the conversation has become too complex for typing. Instead of leaving the chat to go to the Calendar, you can schedule a meeting right from the chat window.

1. Look at the message compose box where you usually type your text.
2. Click the **Schedule a meeting** icon (it looks like a small calendar with a plus sign).
3. This opens a simplified version of the scheduling window. Since you are initiating this from a chat, the attendees are often automatically added.
4. Set your time and date, then click **Send**.

## Joining a Meeting

Depending on how the meeting was organized, you will join using one of three common methods.

### Via the Calendar
If you were invited to a meeting, it will appear on your calendar. 
1. Go to the **Calendar tab**.
2. Click once on the meeting block.
3. Click the **Join** button that appears in the pop-up window.

### Via a Meeting Link
You may receive a meeting invitation via email or a chat message that contains a hyperlink (a clickable piece of text) that says **"Click here to join the meeting."**

When you click this link, your computer will ask how you want to join:
*   **Download the Windows/Mac app:** Best for the full experience and stability.
*   **Continue on this browser:** This opens the meeting in a web browser (like Chrome or Edge). This is ideal if you are on a computer that isn't yours or if you don't have the app installed.
*   **Open your Teams app:** If you already have the app installed, this is the fastest route.

### Via a Channel
If a meeting is scheduled within a specific **Channel** (the organized spaces we explored in Chapter 4), it is visible to everyone in that team. You will see a "Join" button appear directly in the channel's conversation feed when the meeting starts. Anyone in that team can jump in without needing a personal calendar invite.

## Mastering the Meeting Controls

Once you enter a meeting, you are presented with the **Meeting Control Bar**. This is the toolbar that allows you to manage your presence and interaction.

### Audio and Video Basics
Before you fully enter the meeting, Teams shows you a "pre-join" screen. Here, you can toggle your **Camera** and **Microphone** on or off so you aren't surprised by your appearance or background noise the moment you join.

Once inside, use these buttons on the control bar:
*   **Mute/Unmute (Microphone icon):** Click this to silence your microphone. It is a professional courtesy to stay muted when you aren't speaking to prevent background noise (like typing or dogs barking) from distracting others.
*   **Camera On/Off (Video icon):** Click this to turn your webcam on or off.

### Meeting Chat
Just like the text chats in Chapter 5, every meeting has its own dedicated chat. 
1. Click the **Chat** icon on the control bar.
2. A panel will slide open on the right side of the screen.
3. You can use this to share links, ask questions without interrupting the speaker, or send a quick "I'll be right back" message.

### Screen Sharing
**Screen sharing** allows you to show other participants what is on your monitor. This is essential for presentations or demonstrating a process.

1. Click the **Share** icon (an arrow pointing up inside a square).
2. You will be given two main choices:
    *   **Screen:** This shares your entire desktop. Warning: Everyone will see everything, including your notifications and other open folders.
    *   **Window:** This allows you to pick one specific app (like a PowerPoint presentation or an Excel sheet). This is more private and focused.
3. To stop sharing, click the **Stop sharing** button that appears in the small control window.

## Recording a Meeting

There are times when a team member cannot attend, or you need a permanent record of a decision. This is where the **Record** feature comes in.

### How to Start a Recording
1. While in the meeting, click the **More** button (the three dots `...`) on the control bar.
2. Hover over **Record and transcribe**.
3. Select **Start recording**.

**Important:** When you start recording, Teams will send a notification to every participant letting them know they are being recorded. This ensures privacy and transparency.

### Finding the Recording Afterward
You don't need to hunt through your folders to find the video. Teams stores recordings automatically:
*   **In the Meeting Chat:** Once the meeting ends, the recording will appear as a thumbnail in the chat history of that meeting.
*   **In the Channel:** If the meeting was held in a channel, the recording will be posted in the channel conversation.
*   **In File Storage:** The recording is saved to the cloud (OneDrive or SharePoint), which means you can share the link with people who weren't even invited to the original meeting.

## Inviting External Guests

Microsoft Teams is not limited to people inside your own organization. You can invite "Guests"—people with different email addresses (like a client, a vendor, or a partner).

### Using a Meeting Link
The simplest way to bring an external person into a meeting is by sending them the **Join Link**.

1. Schedule the meeting as usual via the **Calendar tab**.
2. Once the meeting is created, open the event on your calendar.
3. You will see a link that says **"Click here to join the meeting."**
4. Right-click that link and select **Copy Link**.
5. Paste that link into an email or a calendar invite for the external guest.

When the guest clicks the link, they can join via their web browser without needing to create a Microsoft account or install the Teams app. They will be placed in a "Lobby" (a virtual waiting room) until you or another organizer clicks **Admit** to let them into the meeting.

## Key Takeaways

*   **Scheduling Flexibility:** Use the **Calendar tab** for formal planning or the **Chat** window for quick, spontaneous meetings.
*   **Joining Options:** You can join via the app, a web browser, or directly from a channel conversation.
*   **Control Your Presence:** Use the **Mute** and **Camera** toggles to manage your audio and video, and the **Share** button to show your screen or a specific window.
*   **Preserving Information:** Use the **Record** feature via the "More" menu to save the meeting; the video is automatically stored in the meeting chat.
*   **External Access:** Guests can join meetings via a **Join Link** and can participate through a browser without needing the full software installed.

# Chapter 9: Using Audio and Video Features During Meetings

## Avoiding the "Can You Hear Me?" Moment

Imagine this: You’ve just joined a high-stakes project meeting. You begin explaining a critical update, speaking passionately for two full minutes, only to be interrupted by a colleague saying, "Sorry, you're on mute, we couldn't hear a word." 

It is a common, slightly embarrassing experience in the world of remote work. However, mastering your audio and video settings transforms a meeting from a technical struggle into a professional presentation. When you control your environment and your tools, you can focus entirely on the conversation rather than worrying if your camera is angled correctly or if your microphone is picking up the sound of your neighbor's lawnmower.

## Pre-Flight Checks: Adjusting Settings Before You Join

The most stressful time to fix a technical glitch is *after* you have already entered a meeting with ten other people watching. Microsoft Teams provides a "pre-join" screen—a digital dressing room of sorts—where you can verify your equipment before anyone else sees or hears you.

### The Pre-Join Screen
When you click a link to join a meeting (as learned in *Starting and Joining Meetings in Teams*), you aren't dropped immediately into the call. Instead, you see a preview window. This is your opportunity to perform a "pre-flight check."

1.  **The Video Toggle:** You will see a switch to turn your camera on or off. If you aren't camera-ready, keep this off.
2.  **The Audio Toggle:** Similarly, you can mute or unmute your microphone before entering.
3.  **Device Settings:** Look for the gear icon or the "Device settings" link. This is where you tell Teams exactly which hardware to use.

### Selecting Your Hardware
If you have a headset plugged in but Teams is using your laptop's built-in microphone, your audio may sound echoey or distant. In **Device Settings**, you can choose:

*   **Speaker:** Where the sound comes *out* (e.g., your headphones or laptop speakers).
*   **Microphone:** Where the sound goes *in* (e.g., your headset mic or laptop mic).
*   **Camera:** Which lens to use (relevant if you have an external webcam plugged into your computer).

**Pro Tip:** If you aren't sure if your mic is working, look for the small volume bar next to the microphone selection. As you speak, the bar should move, indicating that Teams is detecting your voice.

## Managing Your Visual Presence

Video is a powerful tool for building rapport, but your surroundings aren't always professional. Whether you are working from a home office with laundry in the background or a noisy coffee shop, Teams offers tools to control what others see.

### Background Effects and Blur
**Background effects** allow you to hide your actual physical environment and replace it with a digital image or a blur.

**How to apply these effects:**
*   **Before joining:** On the pre-join screen, select "Background filters."
*   **During a meeting:** Click the "More" button (the three dots `...`) in the meeting toolbar and select "Effects and avatars" $\rightarrow$ "Video effects."

You have three primary options:
1.  **Blur:** This keeps you in focus but softens everything behind you into a smudge. This is the best choice for a professional, neutral look.
2.  **Standard Backgrounds:** Teams provides several built-in images, such as a modern office or a cozy living room.
3.  **Custom Backgrounds:** You can upload your own image (such as a company logo or a professional photo of an office) by clicking "Add new."

### Camera Etiquette
While the technology allows you to stay on camera, "video fatigue" is real. A good rule of thumb for beginners:
*   **Keep your camera on** during small team syncs or one-on-one meetings to maintain a human connection.
*   **Turn your camera off** during very large presentations or when you are focusing intensely on a document being shared, unless you are the one speaking.

## Enhancing Accessibility with Live Captions

Not every meeting environment is perfect. You might be in a noisy room, or you may be collaborating with a colleague whose first language is different from yours. **Live Captions** solve this by providing a real-time text transcription of what is being said.

### Enabling Live Captions
Live captions do not record the meeting for everyone; they are a personal setting that only you can see.

1.  While in a meeting, click the **More** (`...`) icon in the toolbar.
2.  Navigate to **Language and speech**.
3.  Select **Turn on live captions**.

Once enabled, a text feed will appear at the top or bottom of your screen. Teams will attempt to identify who is speaking and display their words in real-time.

**Important Note on Language:** For captions to be accurate, Teams needs to know what language is being spoken. If the captions look like gibberish, go back to the "Language and speech" menu and ensure the "Spoken language" is set correctly (e.g., English (United States)).

## Participating in Large Meetings

In a small chat, it's easy to find a gap in the conversation to speak. In a meeting with 20 or more people, jumping in can lead to people talking over one another, which creates audio "clashing" and frustration.

### The Raise Hand Feature
The **Raise Hand** feature is a digital signal to the meeting organizer that you have a question or a comment, without interrupting the current speaker.

**How to use it:**
1.  Click the **Raise** button (the hand icon) in the meeting toolbar.
2.  You will see a small hand icon appear next to your name/video feed.
3.  The organizer or speaker will see a list of everyone who has their hand raised and can call on you in the order you joined the queue.
4.  Once you have finished speaking, remember to click the hand icon again to **lower your hand**.

### Using the Chat for Side-Channel Communication
Remember the **Text chats** discussed in earlier chapters? During a meeting, the chat remains available. If you have a thought that isn't urgent enough to "Raise Hand" for, type it into the meeting chat. This allows the speaker to address your point at the end of their presentation without breaking their flow.

## Sharing Your Screen and Content

Often, the best way to explain a concept is to *show* it. Whether it's a spreadsheet, a PowerPoint presentation, or a website, Teams allows you to project your screen to all other participants.

### Understanding Share Options
When you click the **Share** button (the square with an upward arrow), Teams will ask you what exactly you want to share. This is a critical choice for your privacy.

**1. Screen Sharing (Entire Screen)**
This shares everything you see on your monitor. If you have two monitors, you can choose which one to share.
*   **When to use it:** When you need to switch between multiple different apps (e.g., moving from a website to an Excel sheet).
*   **The Risk:** Everyone will see your desktop icons, your taskbar, and—most importantly—any incoming notifications (like a private chat message) that pop up in the corner of your screen.

**2. Window Sharing (Specific App)**
This shares only one specific application window.
*   **When to use it:** When you only want people to see your PowerPoint presentation, but you want to keep your email or private notes hidden on the rest of your screen.
*   **The Benefit:** Even if you switch to another app on your own screen, the audience will still only see the window you originally selected.

### Sharing Audio
If you are sharing a video clip (like a YouTube video or a recorded demo), you must tell Teams to include the sound. 

When you click the **Share** button, look for the toggle switch labeled **Include computer sound**. If you forget to flip this switch, your audience will see the video moving, but they will hear total silence.

### Stopping the Share
To stop sharing, simply hover your mouse over the top of the shared screen to find the **Stop sharing** button (the "X" icon), or click the "Stop sharing" button in the main meeting toolbar.

## Realistic Scenario: The Monthly Project Review

Let's put these features into practice with a realistic scenario. 

**The Situation:** Sarah is a beginner Teams user. She is presenting a monthly progress report to her manager and five other colleagues. She is working from home and her living room is visible behind her.

**The Workflow:**
1.  **The Pre-Join:** Sarah joins the meeting. On the pre-join screen, she checks her **Device Settings** to ensure her headset is selected so the others don't hear her dog barking.
2.  **The Privacy:** She notices her laundry pile in the background, so she selects the **Blur** background effect before clicking "Join now."
3.  **The Presentation:** When it's her turn to speak, Sarah clicks **Share**. She chooses **Window** and selects her PowerPoint presentation—this ensures her manager doesn't see the personal emails she has open in another window.
4.  **The Interaction:** While Sarah is speaking, a colleague uses the **Raise Hand** feature. Sarah sees the notification, finishes her current slide, and then answers the colleague's question.
5.  **The Accessibility:** One colleague is joining from a loud airport and enables **Live Captions** so they can follow Sarah's presentation despite the noise around them.

## Key Takeaways

*   **Pre-Join is for Preparation:** Use the pre-join screen to test your microphone, camera, and speakers before entering the meeting.
*   **Control Your Environment:** Use **Blur** or **Background images** to maintain professional privacy.
*   **Prioritize Accessibility:** Use **Live Captions** to help with noise interference or language barriers.
*   **Respect the Flow:** Use the **Raise Hand** feature in larger meetings to signal you want to speak without interrupting.
*   **Share Intentionally:** Use **Window sharing** instead of **Screen sharing** to protect your privacy and avoid distracting the audience with notifications.
*   **Don't Forget the Sound:** Always toggle **Include computer sound** if you are sharing a video.

# Chapter 10: Managing Notifications and Settings for a Smoother Experience

## The Battle Against the "Ping"

Imagine this: You are in the middle of drafting an important report. You’ve finally hit your stride, your thoughts are flowing, and you are deeply focused. Suddenly, a small rectangular box pops up in the corner of your screen. *Ping!* A colleague has asked a question in a general channel. *Ping!* Another teammate has shared a file. *Ping!* A group chat is debating where to go for lunch.

Within three minutes, your concentration is shattered. You spend the next twenty minutes responding to non-urgent messages, and by the time you return to your report, you've forgotten where you left off.

This is the paradox of the modern digital workspace. While Microsoft Teams is designed to reduce friction in collaboration, the very tools that keep us connected—notifications—can become the biggest obstacles to our productivity. The secret to mastering Teams is not just knowing how to use its features, but knowing how to silence them.

## Understanding Notifications

A **notification** is a digital alert that tells you something has happened in Teams. These can take several forms:

*   **Banners:** The small pop-up windows that appear in the bottom-right corner of your screen.
*   **Activity Feed:** The "bell" icon in the top-left of your interface that lists everything requiring your attention.
*   **Badge:** The small red circle with a number that appears on the Teams icon in your taskbar or on the Activity feed.
*   **Email:** Messages sent to your Outlook inbox when you have been away from Teams for a while.

The goal is to move from "Notification Chaos" (getting alerted for everything) to "Intentional Awareness" (getting alerted only for what actually matters).

## Global Notification Settings

Before tweaking specific channels, it is helpful to set your general preferences. This ensures that the "default" behavior of the app matches your working style.

### Accessing the Settings Menu
To reach the main control center:
1. Click the **three dots (...)** (Settings and more) located next to your profile picture in the top-right corner of the Teams window.
2. Select **Settings** from the dropdown menu.
3. Click on **Notifications** in the left-hand sidebar.

### Customizing Your Alerts
In the Notifications menu, you will see a list of different activity types (e.g., Chats, Meetings, Calls). For each of these, you can choose how you want to be notified:

*   **Banner and Feed:** The most intrusive. You get a pop-up and an entry in your activity list.
*   **Only in Feed:** Subtle. No pop-up appears, but the item is waiting for you when you click the bell icon.
*   **Off:** You will not be notified of this specific action at all.

**Pro Tip:** For beginners, we recommend setting "Chats" to **Banner and Feed** so you don't miss direct messages, but setting "Community" or "General" alerts to **Only in Feed** to avoid constant interruptions.

## Managing Channel-Specific Notifications

In earlier chapters, we discussed how to organize your workspace into Teams and Channels. Because some channels are high-priority (like "Urgent Project X") and others are low-priority (like "Watercooler Chat"), you should not treat them the same.

### Customizing a Specific Channel
You can override your global settings for any individual channel:
1. Navigate to the **Teams** tab and find the specific channel.
2. Hover over the channel name and click the **three dots (...)** (More options).
3. Select **Channel notifications**.
4. Choose your preference:
    *   **All activity:** You get notified of every single post and reply in that channel. (Use this sparingly!)
    *   **Custom:** This allows you to decide if you want banners for "All new posts" or only when someone uses an **@Mention** to call you specifically.
    *   **Off:** You will only see updates in this channel when you manually click on it.

### The Power of "Muting"
If a specific group chat becomes too noisy—perhaps a long thread of jokes or a brainstorming session that doesn't involve you—you can **Mute** it. 

To mute a chat:
1. Go to the **Chat** tab.
2. Hover over the chat in your list and click the **three dots (...)**.
3. Select **Mute**.

Once muted, you will still receive the messages, but you won't get a banner or a sound. The chat will simply show a "muted" icon, and you can check it at your convenience.

## Controlling Email Notifications

Microsoft Teams is designed to replace internal email, but it can still use email as a backup. This is known as **Missed Activity Emails**.

If you are away from your computer and a message arrives, Teams may send an email to your Microsoft 365 inbox to let you know. For some, this is a helpful safety net; for others, it feels like "double notification" and creates clutter.

### How to adjust these emails:
1. Go to **Settings** $\rightarrow$ **Notifications**.
2. Look for the **Email** section.
3. In the dropdown menu for **Missed activity emails**, you can choose:
    *   **As soon as possible:** Email is sent immediately.
    *   **Every 10 minutes / Every hour:** Teams bundles your missed alerts into one summary email.
    *   **Off:** No emails are sent.

## Managing Your Presence and Availability

Your **Status** is a visual indicator that tells your colleagues whether you are available to talk or if you are focusing on deep work. It is a critical tool for managing expectations.

### Understanding Status Types
When you click your profile picture in the top-right, you will see your current status. The most common options include:

*   **Available (Green):** You are online and ready to collaborate.
*   **Busy (Red):** You are working, but can be interrupted if necessary. Teams often sets this automatically if you have a meeting scheduled in your calendar.
*   **Do Not Disturb (Red with a white bar):** This is the "Deep Work" mode. **Crucially, this mutes all banners.** No pop-ups will appear on your screen, allowing you to focus entirely.
*   **Away (Yellow):** You have been inactive on your computer for several minutes.
*   **Be Right Back:** A manual status to let people know you've stepped away for a moment.

### Setting a Status Message
Sometimes a color isn't enough. A **Status Message** allows you to provide context.

**Scenario:** You are attending a full-day training workshop. You are technically "Online," but you cannot respond to messages.
1. Click your profile picture.
2. Click **Set status message**.
3. Type: *"In training until 5 PM. For urgent issues, please contact Sarah."*
4. Check the box **Show when people message me**. This ensures that as soon as someone starts typing a message to you, your note appears above their text box.
5. Set the "Clear status message after" timer to "Today" so it disappears automatically tomorrow.

## Setting Up Quiet Hours (Quiet Days)

If you use the Teams mobile app on your phone, the line between "work time" and "home time" can blur. To prevent your phone from buzzing during dinner or late at night, you can set **Quiet Hours**.

## Key Takeaways

# Chapter 11: Integrating Apps and Tools with Microsoft Teams

## Stop the "App Switch" Fatigue

Imagine your typical workday: You start a conversation in a **Text chat** in Microsoft Teams, but then you realize you need to check a task status in Trello. You leave Teams, open your browser, find the Trello tab, and update the card. Then, you remember you need to poll your team about a meeting time, so you open a separate polling tool or send five individual messages. Finally, you check an industry news site for an update that affects your project.

By the time you return to Teams to tell your colleagues the news, you’ve switched windows six times. This is known as "context switching," and it is a productivity killer.

The power of Microsoft Teams is that it isn't just a place for chatting and meetings; it is a **digital workspace** designed to act as a central hub. Instead of you going to your tools, you can bring your tools to you. By integrating third-party apps and connectors, you can manage projects, track data, and automate updates without ever leaving the Teams interface.

## Understanding Apps and Connectors

Before diving into the "how," it is important to understand the two primary ways Teams brings in outside information: **Apps** and **Connectors**.

### What are Teams Apps?
An **App** in Microsoft Teams is a piece of software that adds a specific functionality to your workspace. Some are built by Microsoft (like the Calendar or Tasks app), while others are built by third parties (like Trello, Asana, or Polly). 

Apps can live in three different places:
1.  **Personal:** Only you can see and use the app (e.g., a personal To-Do list).
2.  **Chat:** The app helps you and a few others during a private conversation.
3.  **Team/Channel:** The app is available to everyone in a specific channel, creating a shared tool for the whole group.

### What are Connectors?
While an app is an interactive tool, a **Connector** is more like a "notification pipe." A connector allows an external service to push information *into* a Teams channel. 

For example, instead of checking a website every hour for news, you can use an **RSS Feed connector** (Really Simple Syndication—a standardized web feed) to automatically post a link in a channel whenever a new article is published. Connectors are generally "read-only" streams of information, whereas apps are interactive.

## Browsing and Installing Apps

The **Teams App Store** is the central library where you can find tools to enhance your workflow.

### How to Find Apps
1.  Look at the left-hand navigation bar (the "App Bar") in your Teams window.
2.  Click on the **Apps** icon at the bottom of the list.
3.  Use the **Search bar** at the top left to look for a specific tool (e.g., "Polly" or "Trello"), or browse the categories provided by Microsoft.

### Installing an App
Once you find an app you want to use, click on it. You will typically see two options:
*   **Add:** This adds the app to your personal view.
*   **Add to a team:** This allows you to select a specific Team and Channel where the app will be available for everyone.

**Note on Permissions:** Depending on your organization's settings, some apps may require "Admin Approval." If you see a message saying you need permission, you will have to request the app through your company's IT department.

## Adding Apps to Teams and Channels

Adding an app to a channel transforms that channel from a simple conversation thread into a functional workstation. Let's look at three common types of integrations.

### Project Management (Trello or Asana)
If your team uses Trello or Asana to track tasks, you don't need to keep a browser window open. By adding these apps to a channel, you can:
*   View your project board directly within a Teams tab.
*   Post a specific task card into a chat for discussion.
*   Update task statuses without leaving the conversation.

### Quick Feedback (Polly)
**Polly** is a popular app used for creating instant polls and surveys. Instead of asking "Does Tuesday work for everyone?" and scrolling through ten different answers, you can launch a Polly poll. Team members simply click their choice, and the results are tallied automatically in the chat.

### Step-by-Step: Adding an App to a Channel
1.  Navigate to the **Channel** where you want the app.
2.  Click the **(+) plus icon** (Add a tab) located at the top of the channel window.
3.  Search for the app (e.g., "Polly" or "Trello").
4.  Follow the on-screen prompts to sign in to that service.
5.  Click **Save**. The app now appears as a **Tab** at the top of the channel.

## Using Connectors for External Data

Connectors are ideal for teams that need to stay updated on external triggers without manually checking multiple websites.

### Scenario: The Industry Watchdog
Imagine you are on a Marketing Team. You need to know the moment a competitor publishes a new blog post or when a specific keyword is mentioned in a news feed. Instead of assigning someone to check these sites daily, you can set up an **RSS Feed Connector**.

### How to Set Up a Connector
1.  Go to the channel you want the data to flow into.
2.  Click the **three dots (...)** (More options) next to the channel name.
3.  Select **Connectors**.
4.  Browse the list of available connectors (e.g., RSS, GitHub, Jira, or Mailchimp).
5.  Click **Add** and enter the required information (such as the URL of the RSS feed).
6.  Click **Create**.

Now, whenever that external source updates, a formatted message will automatically appear in the channel, alerting everyone instantly.

## Pinning Apps for Quick Access

As you add more tools to your workspace, your navigation bar can become cluttered. **Pinning** allows you to prioritize the apps you use most frequently.

### Pinning to the App Bar
If you use an app (like "Tasks by Planner") every single day, you don't want to search for it in the App Store every time.
1.  Right-click the app icon in the left-hand navigation bar.
2.  Select **Pin**.
3.  The app will now stay permanently visible in your sidebar, regardless of which team or chat you are currently viewing.

### Pinning to a Channel (Tabs)
When you add an app to a channel using the **(+) plus icon**, it is automatically "pinned" as a tab at the top. This ensures that any new member who joins the channel can immediately see the project board or the shared tool without having to ask where it is located.

## Managing and Uninstalling Apps

Your digital workspace should evolve. A tool that was useful for a three-month project may become "noise" once the project is complete. Removing unused apps keeps your interface clean and reduces distractions.

### How to Remove an App from a Channel
1.  Go to the channel containing the app.
2.  Click the **dropdown arrow** next to the app's tab name at the top of the screen.
3.  Select **Remove**.
4.  Confirm the removal. This removes the tab for everyone in that channel.

### How to Uninstall a Personal App
1.  Right-click the app icon in your left-hand navigation bar.
2.  Select **Uninstall**.
3.  The app will be removed from your personal view.

## Key Takeaways

*   **Integration** allows you to bring third-party tools into Teams, reducing the need to switch between different windows and browsers.
*   **Apps** are interactive tools (like Polly for polls or Trello for tasks) that can be used personally or shared within a channel.
*   **Connectors** are one-way streams of information (like RSS feeds) that push external updates into a channel.
*   **Tabs** are created when you add an app to a channel, providing a permanent, pinned location for that tool.
*   **Pinning** ensures your most-used apps are always one click away in the left-hand navigation bar.
*   **App Management** involves removing tools that are no longer serving the team's purpose to maintain a streamlined workspace.

# Chapter 12: Best Practices for Organizing and Managing Teams Efficiently

## The Chaos of the "Quick Setup"

Imagine this: You are hired as a project manager for a new product launch. On your first day, you are added to five different Teams. Inside each Team, there are twenty channels with names like "General," "Stuff," "Updates," "Project X," and "Project X Final." You find three different channels where people are discussing the same budget spreadsheet, and you can't tell which one is the current conversation. You spend your first two hours just searching for a file that someone mentioned was "in the channel."

This is what happens when Microsoft Teams is used as a dumping ground rather than a structured workspace. Because the platform makes it so easy to create new spaces, many organizations fall into the trap of "organic growth"—creating Teams and channels on the fly without a plan. The result is digital clutter that slows everyone down.

Efficient management isn't about using every feature available; it is about creating a predictable system so your team spends less time searching for information and more time doing the actual work.

## Planning Your Structure Before You Build

The biggest mistake beginners make is clicking "Create Team" the moment they have an idea. Once a Team is populated with members and files, changing the fundamental structure becomes disruptive. Instead, treat your Teams structure like a blueprint for a house: plan the rooms before you start nailing boards together.

### Defining the "Team" vs. the "Channel"
To plan effectively, you must first decide the scope of your containers. 

*   **A Team** should represent a large, stable group of people who share a common identity or long-term goal. Examples include a Department (Marketing), a permanent Project (Website Redesign 2024), or a functional group (Executive Leadership).
*   **A Channel** should represent a specific topic, a workstream, or a phase of a project within that Team. If a Team is the "house," Channels are the "rooms."

### The Planning Process
Before creating anything in the interface, grab a piece of paper or a digital notepad and answer these three questions:

1.  **Who needs to be here?** If the group of people changes every week, you might need a different structure. If the group is stable, they belong in a Team.
2.  **What are the primary "buckets" of conversation?** List the main topics the group discusses. These will become your channels.
3.  **Is this temporary or permanent?** A project that ends in three months should be structured differently than a department that will exist for years.

**Scenario: The Event Planning Committee**
If you are organizing a large corporate conference, don't create a separate *Team* for "Catering," "Speakers," and "Venue." That would force your core committee members to jump between three different Teams constantly. 

Instead:
*   **Create one Team:** "Annual Conference 2024"
*   **Create Channels for the topics:** "Venue & Logistics," "Speaker Coordination," "Catering & Menu," and "Marketing & Tickets."

This keeps the entire project in one place while keeping the conversations categorized.

## Mastering Naming Conventions

In a large organization, you might eventually be a member of dozens of Teams. When you look at your sidebar, "Project A" and "Project B" aren't helpful if you have five different "Project A's" across different departments. 

A **Naming Convention** is a standardized way of naming your Teams and Channels so that anyone can understand what they are and who they belong to without having to click on them.

### Tips for Naming Teams
Avoid vague names. Use a prefix system to group similar Teams together visually.

*   **Bad:** "Marketing" (Too vague)
*   **Better:** "DEPT-Marketing" (Tells the user this is a Departmental team)
*   **Bad:** "Website" (Which website? Which year?)
*   **Better:** "PROJ-Website-Redesign-2024" (Tells the user this is a Project team with a specific timeframe)

### Tips for Naming Channels
Channels should be descriptive and action-oriented. Avoid naming channels "General" for everything (though Teams creates a General channel by default, try to use it only for high-level announcements).

*   **Avoid:** "Files" or "Chat" (Everything in Teams has files and chat; these names add no value).
*   **Use:** "Budget-Approvals," "Client-Feedback," or "Weekly-Sync-Notes."

**Pro Tip:** Use hyphens or underscores instead of spaces if your organization integrates Teams with other legacy software, as this prevents technical errors in file paths.

## Maintaining a Tidy Workspace

Digital workspaces suffer from "entropy"—the tendency for things to become disorganized over time. To prevent this, you must actively manage the lifecycle of your Teams.

### Archiving Inactive Teams
When a project ends, do not simply leave the Team sitting there. If you have ten "dead" Teams in your list, you will struggle to find the active ones. 

**Archiving** is the process of putting a Team into a "read-only" state. When you archive a Team:
1.  The Team remains visible, but members cannot start new conversations or edit files.
2.  The historical data is preserved for future reference.
3.  It signals to everyone that the project is officially closed.

Check your Team list once a quarter. If a Team hasn't had a post in 30 days and the project is complete, archive it.

### Reviewing Permissions and Memberships
Over time, "membership creep" happens. People join a Team for a specific task, the task ends, but they remain in the Team, receiving notifications for things that no longer concern them.

Set a recurring calendar reminder (e.g., every three months) to perform a **Membership Audit**:
*   **Remove** people who have changed roles or left the project.
*   **Update** owners. Every Team should have at least two owners so that if one person leaves the company, the Team isn't left "orphaned" without an administrator.
*   **Verify** private channels. Ensure that only the necessary people have access to sensitive channels.

## Establishing Team Etiquette

Microsoft Teams is a powerful tool, but it can become a source of stress if the team doesn't agree on *how* to use it. Without etiquette, the "Persistent chat" nature of the platform can lead to notification fatigue.

As the manager or creator of a Team, you should establish a "Working Agreement" or a set of guidelines. Share these in the **General** channel and pin them to the top.

### Recommended Etiquette Guidelines

**1. The "Right Tool for the Job" Rule**
Train your team to choose the communication method based on urgency and complexity:
*   **Urgent/Quick Question:** Use a Chat.
*   **Project-related Discussion:** Use a Channel conversation.
*   **Complex Problem/Emotional Topic:** Use a Voice or Video call.
*   **Formal Announcement:** Use a post in the General channel.

**2. Threading Conversations**
One of the most common beginner mistakes is starting a new conversation for every single reply. This creates a long, fragmented wall of text. 
*   **The Rule:** Always use the **Reply** button beneath a post to keep the conversation in a "thread." This keeps the topic grouped together and prevents the channel from becoming a chaotic stream of unrelated messages.

**3. Mindful @Mentions**
As covered in previous chapters, @mentions are great for getting attention, but overusing them creates "noise."
*   **The Rule:** Avoid using `@Team` or `@Channel` unless the information is critical for *everyone* in that group. If you only need an answer from Sarah, @mention Sarah specifically.

**4. Status Respect**
Teach team members to respect the status indicators (Available, Busy, Do Not Disturb). 
*   **The Rule:** If someone is marked as "Do Not Disturb," avoid sending urgent pings unless it is a genuine emergency.

## Putting it All Together: The Management Checklist

To ensure your Teams stay efficient, follow this recurring maintenance cycle:

| Frequency | Action | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Daily** | Encourage threading in conversations | Prevents channel clutter. |
| **Weekly** | Pin important files or posts to the top | Ensures key info is easy to find. |
| **Monthly** | Review channel names and structure | Adjusts for evolving project needs. |
| **Quarterly** | Archive dead Teams & audit memberships | Keeps the sidebar clean and secure. |

## Key Takeaways

*   **Plan Before Creating:** Define the scope of your Team (the "who") and your Channels (the "what") before building to avoid structural chaos.
*   **Standardize Naming:** Use prefixes (e.g., DEPT- or PROJ-) to make Teams and Channels instantly recognizable and searchable.
*   **Fight Clutter:** Archive inactive Teams to keep your workspace focused and perform regular membership audits to remove unnecessary users.
*   **Set Expectations:** Establish a Team Etiquette agreement to ensure members use threads correctly and @mentions sparingly.
*   **Manage the Lifecycle:** Treat your digital workspace like a physical office; it requires regular cleaning and reorganization to remain productive.

# Chapter 13: Collaborating with External Guests and Partners in Teams

## The "Outside-In" Collaboration Challenge

Imagine you are managing a project to redesign your company’s website. You have your internal team of designers and writers, but you’ve hired an external marketing agency to handle the SEO (Search Engine Optimization) and a freelance copywriter to polish the text.

Up until now, your communication with these partners has been a chaotic mix of long email threads, scattered PDF attachments, and "Can you send me the latest version?" messages. You want them to have access to your project's **File storage and collaboration** tools and participate in **Persistent conversations**, but you cannot—and should not—give them a full employee account with access to your company's internal payroll or HR folders.

This is where **Guest Access** comes in. It allows you to open a secure window into your digital workspace, inviting specific people from outside your organization to collaborate without compromising the privacy of your entire company.

## Understanding Guests vs. Members

Before you send an invite, it is important to understand the distinction between a **Member** and a **Guest**. In Microsoft Teams, these roles determine what a person can see and do.

### What is a Member?
A Member is someone within your own organization. They have a full Microsoft 365 account provided by your company. They can create their own Teams, build channels, and have full access to the organization's internal directory.

### What is a Guest?
A **Guest** is someone from outside your organization (like a client, vendor, or freelancer) who is invited to collaborate. They use their own existing email address (whether it is from another company or a personal account like Gmail or Outlook) to sign in.

**Guest Permissions and Limitations**
To keep your organization secure, Guests have a restricted set of capabilities. While they can do most of the "work," they cannot perform "administrative" tasks.

**What Guests CAN do:**
* Participate in **Text chats** and **Voice and video calls**.
* Create and edit files in the **File storage and collaboration** areas of the Team they were invited to.
* Use **@mentions** to get someone's attention.
* Join scheduled meetings.

**What Guests CANNOT do:**
* Create their own Teams or Channels.
* Remove other members or guests from a Team.
* Access the organization's full internal directory (they can only see people within the Team they have joined).
* Use certain internal-only apps integrated into your Teams environment.

## How to Invite an External Guest

Inviting a guest is a straightforward process, but it happens at the **Team** level. You cannot invite a guest to a "company" generally; you must invite them to a specific space.

### Step-by-Step: Adding a Guest to a Team
1. Open Microsoft Teams and locate the Team you want the guest to join.
2. Click the **More options (...)** icon next to the Team name.
3. Select **Add member**.
4. Type the guest's full email address. 
5. As you type, Teams will recognize that the email is external and display a message: *"Add [Email Address] as a guest."* Click on that suggestion.
6. Click **Add**.

Once you click add, Microsoft Teams sends an email invitation to the guest. The guest must accept this invitation to gain access to the Team.

### Inviting Guests to a Specific Channel
Sometimes, you don't want a partner to see everything in a Team. For example, you might have a "Website Redesign" Team with a "Budget" channel (internal only) and a "Feedback" channel (open to guests).

To achieve this, you must use a **Private Channel**. When you create a private channel, you can invite a specific subset of the Team's members—including guests—to that specific channel. If a guest is only added to a private channel, they will not see the general conversations or files in the rest of the Team.

## Collaborating with Guests in Action

Once your guest has accepted the invitation and joined your workspace, the experience is very similar to working with a colleague, but there are a few nuances to keep in mind.

### Using @mentions with Guests
As you learned in previous chapters, **@mentions** are the best way to ensure someone sees a message. This works exactly the same for guests. If you need the external copywriter to review a document, type `@Name` in the chat. 

Because guests are not part of your daily internal flow, @mentions are critical. Without them, a guest might not realize there is a task waiting for them, as they aren't immersed in your company's internal culture and notification habits.

### Sharing and Co-editing Files
One of the biggest advantages of guest access is the ability to use **File sharing and co-editing**. Instead of emailing a Word document back and forth, you can upload the file to the **Files** tab of the channel.

When a guest opens a file in Teams, they can edit it in real-time alongside you. You will see their cursor moving and their changes appearing instantly. This eliminates "version conflict" (where two people edit different versions of the same file) and ensures everyone is working from a single source of truth.

### The "Tenant" Switch
For the guest, using your Team requires a "Tenant Switch." A **Tenant** is essentially the "digital house" of an organization. 

If a guest is a member of their own company's Teams and is also a guest in yours, they will see a dropdown menu in the top-right corner of their Teams app. To talk to you, they must switch from their "Home" tenant to your "Guest" tenant. If a guest tells you they "can't find the chat," it is often because they are still logged into their own company's tenant rather than yours.

## Managing and Removing Guest Access

Access should never be permanent. For security and organization, you should treat guest access as a "temporary pass."

### When to Remove a Guest
You should remove guest access when:
* The project or contract has ended.
* The person has left their company.
* The specific task they were hired for is complete.

### How to Remove a Guest
1. Go to the Team name and click **More options (...)**.
2. Select **Manage team**.
3. Scroll down to the **Members and guests** list.
4. Find the guest's name, click the **X** or the "Remove" option next to their name.
5. Confirm the removal.

Once removed, the guest instantly loses access to all chats, files, and channels within that Team. They will no longer be able to see the Team in their tenant list.

## Troubleshooting Common Guest Issues

Working with external partners occasionally runs into technical friction. Here are the most common hurdles and how to solve them.

**Issue: The guest says they never received the invitation email.**
* **Solution:** Ask them to check their "Junk" or "Spam" folder. If it's not there, go to **Manage team**, remove the guest, and re-add them. Ensure there were no typos in the email address.

**Issue: The guest can't access a specific file.**
* **Solution:** Check the folder permissions. If you moved the file into a **Private Channel** that the guest isn't a member of, they will be blocked. Ensure the file is located in a channel the guest has been explicitly invited to.

**Issue: The guest is confused about where to find the conversation.**
* **Solution:** Remind them to check their **Tenant Switcher** in the top-right corner of Teams. Explain that they are "visiting" your organization's workspace and must switch views to see your messages.

**Issue: You try to add a guest, but Teams says "We couldn't find any matches."**
* **Solution:** This is usually not a problem with the email address, but a restriction set by your company's IT administrator. Some organizations disable guest access for security reasons. If this happens, you will need to contact your IT department to ask if guest access is enabled for your account.

## Key Takeaways

* **Guests** are external users with limited permissions compared to **Members**.
* **Guest Access** allows external partners to participate in chats, calls, and file co-editing without having a full internal account.
* **Invitations** are sent via email and must be accepted by the guest before they can enter the Team.
* **Private Channels** can be used to limit a guest's visibility to only specific parts of a Team.
* **Tenant Switching** is the process guests use to move between their own organization's Teams and yours.
* **Access Management** is crucial; always remove guests once their project is complete to maintain a clean and secure workspace.

# Chapter 14: Security and Privacy Basics in Microsoft Teams

## The Digital Front Door: Why Security Matters in Teams

Imagine you arrive at your office and find that the front door is unlocked, your desk drawers are open, and a stranger is sitting in your chair reading your private notes. You would feel exposed and vulnerable. 

In a digital workspace like Microsoft Teams, your "office" is your account. Because Teams integrates your chats, files, and meetings into one place, it holds a goldmine of sensitive information. If someone gains unauthorized access to your account, they don't just see your messages; they potentially gain access to your company's proprietary data, client lists, and private internal discussions.

Security isn't just the responsibility of the IT department; it is a shared practice. By following a few basic steps, you can ensure that your digital front door is locked and that your private information remains private.

## Locking Your Account with Two-Factor Authentication

The first and most important line of defense for your Microsoft 365 account is your password. However, passwords can be stolen through data breaches or guessed via "brute force" (where a computer program tries thousands of combinations per second).

To stop a hacker who has your password from entering your account, Microsoft uses **Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)**, also known as **Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)**.

### What is Two-Factor Authentication?
2FA is a security process that requires two different forms of identification to access an account. Think of it like an ATM card: to get money, you need the physical card (something you *have*) and the PIN code (something you *know*). Neither one is enough on its own.

In Teams, 2FA usually combines:
1. **Something you know:** Your password.
2. **Something you have:** A mobile phone that receives a text code or a notification via the **Microsoft Authenticator app**.

### How to Enable and Use 2FA
While your organization may have already enabled this for you, it is important to know how to manage it:

1. Sign in to your **Microsoft 365 account security dashboard** (usually found under "My Account" in your profile settings).
2. Navigate to **Security Info**.
3. Select **Add method** and choose **Authenticator app**.
4. Follow the on-screen prompts to scan a QR code with your phone.

Once enabled, when you sign into Teams on a new device, you will enter your password, and then your phone will buzz. You simply tap "Approve," and you are let in. Even if a hacker in another country steals your password, they cannot enter your account because they don't have your physical phone.

## Managing Your Privacy and Presence

Privacy in Teams is about controlling who sees what and when. Because Teams is a social tool designed for collaboration, it shares some of your information by default to help your colleagues know when you are available.

### Controlling Your Profile Privacy
Your profile contains information like your job title, department, and contact details. In most corporate environments, this information is pulled from the company's global directory. 

To manage how you appear:
* Click on your **Profile Picture** in the top right corner.
* Select your name or **Manage Account**.
* Here, you can update your profile photo and basic details. 

### Understanding and Setting Your Status
Your **Presence Status** is the small colored dot next to your profile picture. It tells your teammates whether you are available for a quick chat or in the middle of a deep-focus task.

* **Available (Green):** You are online and active.
* **Busy (Red):** You are in a meeting or have manually set your status to busy.
* **Do Not Disturb (Red with a white bar):** This is the "deep work" mode. It silences all notifications so you can focus.
* **Away (Yellow):** Your computer has been idle for a few minutes.

**Pro Tip:** To manually change your status, click your profile picture $\rightarrow$ click your current status $\rightarrow$ select the new status from the dropdown. You can also set a **Status Message** (e.g., "Out for lunch, back at 1 PM") which appears when people hover over your name or start a chat with you.

## How Teams Stores Your Information

When you send a message or upload a file, that data doesn't just "float" in the air; it is stored in specific locations within the Microsoft 365 cloud. Understanding this helps you understand who has access to your work.

### Where does the data go?
* **One-on-One Chats:** Messages are stored in the sender's and receiver's hidden folders in Exchange Online (the system that powers Outlook).
* **Channel Conversations:** Messages are stored in the Team's group mailbox.
* **Files in Chats:** When you share a file in a private chat, it is uploaded to your **OneDrive for Business** and shared with the recipient.
* **Files in Channels:** When you upload a file to a channel, it is stored in a **SharePoint** site (the backend storage system for Teams).

### Data Retention Policies
You might wonder: *"If I delete a message, is it gone forever?"*

The answer depends on your organization's **Data Retention Policy**. This is a set of rules created by your IT administrator that determines how long data must be kept for legal or compliance reasons.

* **Retention:** The company may require all chats to be saved for 7 years for legal audits. Even if you "delete" a message from your view, the IT department can still retrieve it from the archives.
* **Deletion:** Some policies automatically delete chats or files after a certain period (e.g., 2 years) to keep the digital workspace clean.

**The Golden Rule:** Always assume that anything written in a professional Teams environment is permanent and discoverable by your organization's administrators.

## Recognizing and Reporting Threats

Because Teams is used for business, it is a target for **Phishing**. Phishing is a fraudulent attempt to obtain sensitive information (like passwords or credit card numbers) by disguising as a trustworthy entity in an electronic communication.

### Red Flags of a Suspicious Message
Even if a message comes through Teams, it could be a threat—especially if it comes from an "External" user (indicated by an "External" tag next to their name). Watch for these signs:

1. **Urgency or Threats:** "Your account will be deleted in 2 hours! Click here to verify."
2. **Unexpected Attachments:** A file named `Invoice_992.zip` from someone you've never spoken to.
3. **Strange Requests:** A "manager" asking you to buy gift cards or send your password via chat.
4. **Mismatched Links:** A link that looks like `microsoft-security-update.net` instead of `microsoft.com`.

### How to Report Suspicious Activity
If you encounter a message that feels "off," do not click any links or download any files. Instead:

1. **Hover** over the message to see the options.
2. Click the **three dots (...)** (More options).
3. Select **Report** $\rightarrow$ **Report a suspicious message**.

Reporting the message alerts your IT security team, allowing them to block the sender for the entire company, protecting your colleagues from the same trap.

## Protecting Sensitive Data with Sensitivity Labels

Not all files are created equal. A "Cafeteria Menu" does not need the same protection as a "Quarterly Financial Report." Microsoft Teams uses **Sensitivity Labels** to help you classify and protect your documents.

### What are Sensitivity Labels?
A sensitivity label is a tag applied to a file or a meeting that triggers specific security behaviors. These labels are defined by your organization (e.g., *Public*, *Internal*, *Confidential*, *Highly Confidential*).

### How Labels Protect Your Work
Depending on the label you choose, Teams may automatically apply the following restrictions:

| Label | Typical Effect |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Public** | No restrictions; can be shared with anyone outside the company. |
| **Internal** | Can be shared with anyone inside the company, but not with external guests. |
| **Confidential** | May restrict the ability to download, print, or forward the document. |
| **Highly Confidential** | May encrypt the file so that only specific named people can open it, regardless of where the file is stored. |

### Applying a Label
When you are editing a document (like a Word or Excel file) within Teams:
1. Look for the **Sensitivity** button in the top ribbon (usually near the Home tab).
2. Click the dropdown and select the appropriate label for the content.
3. The label will now follow the file wherever it goes—even if it is downloaded and emailed to someone else.

## Scenario: The New Hire's First Week

Meet Sarah, a new project manager. On her first day, she is eager to get started and ignores the security onboarding. 

* **The Mistake:** Sarah uses a simple password (`Sarah123!`) and doesn't set up 2FA because she finds the phone app "annoying." 
* **The Incident:** A week later, Sarah receives a message from "Microsoft Support" (marked as **External**) saying her account has a sync error and asking her to click a link to "Fix Account." She clicks it and enters her password.
* **The Result:** Because she didn't have 2FA, the attacker now has full access to her account. They enter her Teams, find a file labeled **"Internal"** containing the company's client list, and download it.

**How it could have been avoided:**
1. **2FA:** If Sarah had enabled 2FA, the attacker would have been blocked at the login screen because they didn't have Sarah's phone to approve the sign-in.
2. **Phishing Awareness:** If Sarah had noticed the **External** tag and the urgent tone, she could have reported the message instead of clicking the link.
3. **Sensitivity Labels:** If the client list had been labeled **"Highly Confidential"** with encryption, the attacker wouldn't have been able to open the file even after stealing the account.

## Key Takeaways

* **2FA/MFA** is your strongest defense; it requires both a password and a physical device to grant access.
* **Presence Status** (Available, Busy, Do Not Disturb) helps manage colleague expectations and your own focus.
* **Data Storage** varies: Chats are in Exchange, Channel files are in SharePoint, and Private files are in OneDrive.
* **Retention Policies** mean that "deleted" doesn't always mean "gone"; always maintain professional communication.
* **Phishing** is common; look for the "External" tag, urgent language, and strange links.
* **Sensitivity Labels** allow you to encrypt and restrict files based on how secret the information is.
